NEwes, newes, newes. Newe as the night they are borne in; Excellent newes! Price, Cocks-combe! what price, but the price o' your ears? As if any man uſed to pay for any thing here. A fine youth! This is a finer youth! There he ſpeakes reaſon to you ſir. Nay Gentlemen, bee at peace one with another; wee have enough for you all three, if you dare take upon truſt. From the Moone, ours ſir. By Moone-ſhine, a neerer way I take it. Sir, you are loſt I aſſure you; for ours came to you neither by the way of Cornelius Agrippa, nor Cornelius Drible. No Philoſophers phantaſie. Or brother of the Roſie croſſes intilligence, no forc'd way, but by the neat and cleane power of Poetrie, Who after a world of theſe curious uncertainties, hath em ployed thither a ſervant of hers in ſearch of truth: who has been there— In perſon. Doe not trouble your faith then, for if that buſh of thornes ſhould prove a goodly Grove of Okes; in what caſe were you, and your expectation. Oh! you have an old Wife belike, or your venerable Jerkin there, make much of'hem: Our relation I tell you ſtill is newes. Of a new World, In the Orbe of the Moone. With navigable Seas, and Rivers. With Havens in't, Caſtles, and Port-Townes! Hundreds, and Weapontakes! Forreſts, Parks, Coney-ground, Meadow-paſture, what not? The Ladyes there, play with them inſtead of little Dogges. Yes, but the Coaches are much o'the nature of the Ladies, for they goe onely with wind. See, what is that this muſicke brings, And is ſo carried in the ayre about?
Bold, and brave new! Or the Phant'ſie that begot'hem. Will you heare any newes? Come forward, you ſhould be ſome dull tradeſman by your pigheaded Sconce now, that thinke there's nothing good any where; but what's to be ſold. A Superlative this! Nor any glaſſe of— Methematicians Perſpicill. The Miſtris of all diſcovery. In the Moone. And is this night return'd. Thoſe are ſtale Enſignes o'the Stages, man i'th Moone, de liverd downe to you by muſty Antiquitie, and are of as doubtfull cre dit as the makers. Certaine, and ſure newes. And new creatures in that World. Which is now found to be an Earth inhabited! Varietie of Nations, Polities, Lawes. In-land Cities, Boroughes, Hamlets, Faires, and Markets! They are Pythagorians, all dumbe as fiſhes, for they have no controverſies to exerciſe themſelves in. All the phantaſticall creatures you can thinke of, are there. No, ſome few you ſhall have, that ſigh or whiſtle them ſelves away; and thoſe are preſently hung up by the heeles like Meteors, with Squibs i' their tayles, to give the wiſer ſort warning. There were, but they are all dead of late for want of Taylors. Monſter? none at all; a very familiar thing, like our foole here on earth. And Knights, and Squires. Above all the Hide-parkes in Chriſtendome, farre more hi ding and private, they doe all in clouds there; they walke i'the clouds, they ſit i'the clouds, they lie i'the clouds, they ride and tumble i'the clouds, their very Coaches are clouds. Fame that doth nouriſh the renowne of Kings, And keepes that fayre, which envie would blot out.
Yes, and thanke you too ſir; what's the price of'hem?
Indeed I am all for ſale Gentlemen, you ſay true, I am a Prin ter, and a Printer of Newes; and I doe hearken after'hem, where ever they be at any rates; I'le give any thing for a good Copie now, be't true or falſe, ſo't be newes. Sir that's all one, they were made for the common people; and why ſhould not they ha' their pleaſure in beleeving of lies are made for them, as you have in Paules that make'hem for your ſelves. See mens divers opinions! It is the Printing of'hem makes 'hem news to a great many, who will indeed beleeve nothing but what's in Print. For thoſe I doe keepe my Preſſes, and ſo many Pens going to bring forth wholſome relations, which once in halfe a ſcore yeares (as the age growes forgetfull) I Print over againe with a new date, and they are of excellent uſe. Mr. Chronicler doe not you talke, I ſhall— I dare, I aſſure you.
And I am for matter of State Gentlemen, by conſequence, ſtory, my Chronicle, to fill up my great booke, which muſt bee three Reame of paper at leaſt; I have agreed with my Stationer aforehand to make it ſo big, and I want for ten quire yet. I ha' beene here ever ſince ſeven a clocke i'the morning to get matter for one page, and I thinke I have it compleate; for I have both noted the number, and the capacity of the degrees here; and told twice over how many candles there are i'th roome lighted, which I will ſet you downe to a ſnuffe preciſely, be cauſe I love to give light to poſteritie in the truth of things. Excellent abuſe rather. I dare too, but nothing ſo much as I ha'done; I have beene ſo cheated with falſe relations i'my time, as I ha' found it a far harder thing to correct my booke, then collect it.
Gentlemen, I am neither Printer, nor Chronologer, but one that otherwiſe take pleaſure i'my Pen: A Factor of newes for all the Shieres of England; I doe write my thouſand Letters a weeke ordinary, ſometim twelve hundred, and maintaine the buſineſſe at ſome charge, both to hold up my reputation with mine owne miniſters in Towne, and my friends of correſpondence in the Countrey; I have friends of all rancks, and of all Religions, for which I keepe an anſwering Catalogue of diſpatch; wherein I have my Puritan newes, my Proteſtant newes, and my Pontificiall newes.
And I have hope to erect a Staple for newes ere long, whether all ſhall be brought, and thence againe vented under the name of Staple-newes; and not truſted to your printed Conundrums of the ſerpent in Suſſex, or the witches bidding the Devill to dinner at Derbie: Newes, that when a man ſends them downe to the Shieres where they are ſaid to be done, were never there to be found. I confeſſe it, but it is the Printing I am offended at, I would have no newes printed; for when they are printed they leave to bee newes; while they are written, though they be falſe, they remaine newes ſtill. And I, as much as comes. From the Moone! which way? by ſea? or by Land? Where? which is he? I muſt ſee his Dog at his girdle, and the buſh of thornes at his backe, ere I beleeve it. And has your Poet brought all this? What Innes, or Alehouſes are there there? does he tell you? Why, in travaile a man knowes theſe things without offence; I am ſure if he be a good Poet, hee has diſcover'd a good Taverne in his time. Many, as betwixt your mans Taylor, and your womans Taylor. Ile ſhew you; your Mans Poet may break out ſtrong and deep i'th mouth, as he ſaid of Pindar, Monte decurrens velut amnis. But your Womans Poet muſt flow, and ſtroak the eare, and (as one of them ſayd of himſelfe ſweetly) Muſt write a Verſe as ſmooth, and calm as Creame, In which there is no torrent, nor ſcarce ſtreame. Muſt write a Verſe as ſmooth, and calm as Creame, In which there is no torrent, nor ſcarce ſtreame. No, I could never arrive but to this Remnant. Yes Poſt, upon the Poets horſe for a wager. A fine Lunatique language i'faith; how doe their Lawyers then? How doe they live then? Ha' you Doppers? 'Tis to be hop'd there are women there then? And Lovers as phantaſticke as ours? No ſir? Are there no ſelfe-Lovers there? S'light what lucke is that? we could have ſpar'd them a Colo nie from hence. Then there are Ladies? And ſervants, and Coaches? Ha' they any places of meeting with their Coaches, and take ing the freſh open aire, and then covert when they pleaſe, as in our Hide-Parke, or ſo? And they ha' their new Wells too, and phiſicall waters I hope to viſit all time of yeare? By clouds ſtill?
Like enough; but to your newes Gentlemen, whence come they?
Oh by a Trunck! I know it, a thing no bigger than a Flute-caſe; A neighbour of mine, a ſpectacle-maker, has drawn the Moone through it at the boare of a whiſtle, and made it as great as a Drum-head twentie times, and brought it within the length of this Roome to me, I know not how often. Right, and as well read of you, I'faith: for Cornelius Agrippa has it, In diſco Lunae, there tis found. And his Proſe too i'faith. How might we doe to ſee your Poet? did he undertake this jour ney (I pray you) to the Moone o'foot? Becauſe one of our greateſt Poets (I know not how good a one) went to Endenburgh o' foot, and came backe; marry he has beene reſtive they ſay ever ſince, for we have had nothing from him; he has ſet out nothing I am ſure. Indeed! has he beene there ſince? belike he rid thither then. Tha' ſeen't in print. Excellent! O, I, Moone-Calves! what Monſter is that I pray you? But ha' they no Carmen to meet and breake their Coaches?
Tut, that's no newes; your perplexive Glaſſes are common. No, it will fall out to be Pythagoras way I warrant you, by writing, and reading i'th Moone. Sir, nothing againe Antiquitie I pray you, I muſt not heare ill of Antiquitie. Is he a Mans Poet, or a Womans Poet I pray you? In what language good ſir?
But differing from ours. Gi' your mindes to't a little. Nor were you beſt, I beleeve. Is there any ſuch difference? Ha' you any more on't? Onely by ſignes and geſtures, for they have no articulate voy ces there, but certaine motions to muſicke: all the diſcourſe there is harmonie. A world of Doppers! but they are there as lunatick perſons, walkers onely; that have leave onely to hum, and ha, not daring to pro phecie, or ſtart up upon ſtooles to raiſe doctrine. But none that will hang themſelves for Love, or eate candles ends, or drinke to their Miſtreſſe-eyes, till their owne bid'hem good night, as the Sublunary Lovers doe. I thinke ſome two or three of them live yet, but they are turn'd Moone-Calves by this. Alas! Carmen, they will over a Carman there, as hee will doe a Child here; you ſhall have a Coachman with cheekes like a trum peter, and a wind in his mouth blow him afore him as farre as he can ſee him; or skirre over him with his batts wings a mile and a halfe, ere hee can ſteere his wry necke to looke where he is. Or in a miſt; the miſts are ordinary i'the Moone, a man that owes money there, needs no other protection; onely buy a miſt and walk in't, hee's never diſcern'd, a matter of a Baubee doe's it. And when they ha' taſted the ſprings of pleaſure enough, and bild, and kiſt,, and are readie to come away; the ſhee's only lay certain egges (for they are never with Child there,) and of thoſe egges are diſ cloſed a race of Creatures like men, but are indeed a ſort of Fowle, in part covered with feathers (they call 'hem Volatees ), that hop from Iſland to Iſland, you ſhall ſee a covey of'hen if you pleaſe preſently. Then know, we doe not move theſe wings ſo ſoone, On which our Poet mounted to the Moone Menippus-like; but all twixt it and us, Thus cleares and helpes to the preſentment, thus. VVE have all this while (though the Muſes Heralds ) adventured to tell your Majeſtie no newes; for hitherto we have mov'd rather to your delight, than your beleife. But now be pleaſed to expect a more noble diſcovery worthie of your eare, as the object will be your eye; A race of your owne, form'd, animated, lightned, and heightned by you, who rapt above the Moone far in ſpe culation of your vertues, have remain'd their intranc'd certaine houres, with wonder of the pietie, wiſedome, Majeſty reflected by you, on them, from the Divine light, to which onely you are leſſe. Theſe by how much higher they have beene carried from earth to contemplate your great neſſe, have now conceiv'd the more haſte and hope in this their returne home to approach your goodneſſe; and led by that excellent likeneſſe of your ſelfe, the truth, imitating Procritus endeavour, that all their mo tions be form'd to the muſicke of your peace, and have their ends in your favour, which alone is able to reſolve and thaw the cold they have pre ſently contracted in comming through the colder Region.
Troth, here was enough; tis a pretty piece of Poetrie as'tis.
Would you could heare on, though. Truly I have not askt him that. How? may we beſeech you? Pittie! would you had had the whole piece for a patterne to all Poetrie. Why doe you aske? Like enough, perhaps he has not all in, when he has all in, he he will ſet out (I warrant you) at leaſt thoſe from whom he had it, it is the very ſame party that has beene i'th Moone now. No I aſſure you, he rather flew upon the wings of his Muſe. There are in all but three wayes of going thither; one is Endymions way, by rapture in ſleepe, or a dreame. The other Minipus his way, by wing, which the Poet tooke. The the third, old Empedocles way; who when he leapt into Aetna, having a drie ſeare bodie, and light, the ſmoake took him and whift him up into the Moone, where he lives yet waving up and downe like a feather, all ſoot and embers comming out of that cole-pit; our Poet met him, and talkt with him. O'th deaw o'th Moone like Graſhoppers, and conferre with the Doppers. The brethren of the Roſie-Croſſe have their Colledge within a mile o'the Moone; a Caſtle i'th ayre that runs upon wheeles with a wing'd lanthorne— And zealous women, that will out-grone, the groning wives of Edinburgh. Your Tunbridge, or the Spaw it ſelfe are meere puddle to'em: When the pleaſant moneths o'the yeare come, they all flocke to certaine broken Iſlands which are called there, the Iſles of delight: What elſe? Their Boates are clouds too. Onely one Iſland they have, is call'd the Iſle of the Epecaenes, becauſe there under one Article both kindes are ſignified, for they are fa ſhioned alike, male and female the ſame, not heads and broad hats, ſhort doublets, and long points; neither do they ever untruſſe for diſtinction, but laugh and lie downe in Moone-ſhine, and ſtab with their ponyards; you doe not know the delight of the Epicaenes in Moon-ſhine. Yes faith, tis time to exerciſe their eies, for their eares begin to be wearie.
speeches.1 HE: That he has, I ſhould thinke the worſe of his Verſe elſe.
